newsitem.title: FRANCE: French consumer spending falls, cars sales up.
newsitem.headline: French consumer spending falls, cars sales up.

text.p: French consumer spending on manufactured goods fell in September despite a sharp rise in car sales as people rushed to beat the end of a new-cars-for-old government rebate scheme.

Consumer consumption of manufactured goods dropped 1.5 percent in the month while spending on cars rose 18.8 percent, national statistics institute INSEE reported. Retail sector spending, which excludes cars, fell 5.6 percent.
The strong car sales were overcome by declines in spending on household equipment, textiles, leather and other goods.
INSEE also said consumer spending on manufactured goods in the third quarter as a whole was up 2.6 percent, which helped to lighten the impact of the September drop in some economists' minds.
A finance ministry official said the third quarter rise in spending supported expectations of strong gross domestic product (GDP) growth in the third quarter.

He also said consumption was down last month because there were fewer Saturdays in September this year and that the return-to-school buying splurge had come at the end of August instead of the beginning of September as is usual.
The government car rebate scheme, which expired at the end of September, also accounted for most of the surprise 2.9 percent rise in industrial production in July and August announced on Wednesday.
Economists said the boost to production and consumption would not last past September, making it likely that fourth quarter consumption and production would fall.
"Car sales will drop and the fourth quarter will be extremely disappointing," said Eric Chaney, economist with Morgan Stanley.

"Now we will have a moderate fourth quarter," Credit Lyonnais economist Valerie Asselot said. "There is no rise in purchasing power. If people have bought cars they have bought them with their savings, and they are not going to buy other things this year."

Consumption has been hit by record unemployment of 12.6 percent, which is toughening the task for the already unpopular centre-right government as it struggles to reverse a deep sense of economic disappointment in France.
